uncited: Primitive Representation defines the geometric and appearance attributes of the explicit 3D primitives used to represent a scene in differentiable splatting methods.

It differs from sibling methods by varying the fundamental density function (e.g., half-Gaussians, surfels) or the parameterization of appearance (e.g., Bézier triangles) while maintaining the core splatting pipeline of projection and alpha compositing.
The concept of representing scenes with explicit geometric primitives for differentiable rendering emerged from the need to combine the speed of rasterization with the flexibility of neural fields.
The standard 3D Gaussian Splatting approach [Parent] popularized the use of anisotropic 3D Gaussians as the primary primitive.

Subsequent research explored alternative primitives to address specific limitations such as sharp edges (Bézier Gaussians), surface accuracy (Surfels, Half-Gaussians), and computational efficiency (Conditional Formulations).
The family of Primitive Representations continues to evolve to support diverse applications ranging from static reconstruction to dynamic scenes and texture mapping.
